facts: Arc length: $l = \frac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$, where $\theta$ is the angle at the centre.
Perimeter of a sector: $P = l + 2r$ — the arc plus **both** radii.
A quadrant is the case $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, and a semicircle is the case $\theta = 180^{\circ}$, where the two radii together make the diameter.
Angles at a point add to $360^{\circ}$, so when the **exterior** angle is marked, the angle at the centre is $360^{\circ}$ minus it.
Use the calculator value of $\pi$, keep the working exact, and round only on the last line to the form the question asks for.
steps: Substitute the angle at the centre and the radius.
Evaluate, then round or leave in terms of $\pi$ as asked.

workedExamples.solution_text: The arc length $l$ measures only the curved edge. The perimeter includes the curved edge and both radii: $P=l+2r$.

The arc is $\frac{75}{360}$ of the circumference.
$\begin{align*}l&=\frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r\\l&=\frac{75}{360}\times2\pi(12)\\l&=5\pi\text{ cm}\\l&\approx15.71\text{ cm}\end{align*}$
Equivalently, the diameter is $24\text{ cm}$, so the arc-length calculation is $\frac{75}{360}\times\pi\times24$.

Subtract the exterior angle from $360^\circ$.
$\begin{align*}\theta&=360^\circ-140^\circ\\\theta&=220^\circ\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}l&=\frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r\\l&=\frac{220}{360}\times2\pi(9)\\l&=11\pi\text{ m}\\l&\approx34.56\text{ m}\end{align*}$

Add both radii to the arc length.
$\begin{align*}P&=l+2r\\P&=\frac{144}{360}\times2\pi(10)+2(10)\\P&=(8\pi+20)\text{ cm}\\P&\approx45.1\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

A quadrant has a $90^\circ$ angle at the centre and two straight radii.
$\begin{align*}P&=l+2r\\P&=\frac{90}{360}\times2\pi(8)+2(8)\\P&=(4\pi+16)\text{ m}\\P&\approx28.6\text{ m}\end{align*}$

Half the circumference gives only the curved edge. The straight diameter must also be included. The radius is $12\div2=6\text{ cm}$.
$\begin{align*}P&=l+2r\\P&=\frac{180}{360}\times2\pi(6)+12\\P&=(6\pi+12)\text{ cm}\\P&\approx30.8\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

Use the given fraction of the circumference, then add both radii.
$\begin{align*}P&=l+2r\\P&=\frac58\times2\pi(8)+2(8)\\P&=(10\pi+16)\text{ cm}\\P&\approx47\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A sector has perimeter $28\text{ cm}$ and radius $5\text{ cm}$. Find its angle at the centre to one decimal place. Is a perimeter of $50\text{ cm}$ possible for a sector with the same radius? Justify your answer.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Subtract both radii to find the arc length, then solve the arc-length equation using inverse operations.
$\begin{align*}P&=l+2r\\28&=l+2(5)\\l&=18\text{ cm}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}18&=\frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi(5)\\18\times360&=10\pi\theta\\\theta&=\frac{6480}{10\pi}\\\theta&\approx206.3^\circ\end{align*}$
For a perimeter of $50\text{ cm}$:
$\begin{align*}50&=l+10\\l&=40\text{ cm}\\40&=\frac{\theta}{360}\times10\pi\\\theta&=\frac{40\times360}{10\pi}\\\theta&\approx458.4^\circ\end{align*}$
This is impossible because the angle of a sector cannot exceed $360^\circ$.

mastery.question_text:
A sector has a radius of $20$ cm.
Is it possible for that sector to have a perimeter of $200$ cm?
Justify your answer with working, giving any angle correct to $1$ decimal place.
mastery.solution_text:
$P = l + 2r$
$200 = l + 2(20)$
$l = 160$
$160 = \frac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi(20)$
$\theta = \frac{160\times 360}{2\pi(20)}$
$= 458.4^{\circ}$
No, it is not possible: the angle at the centre of a sector cannot be more than $360^{\circ}$.
